---
title: Customer outcomes
description: "Define customer inactivity, review engagement, and future spending from customer attributes and related events."
engine: markdown
---

Suppose you have a retailer's customer profiles, transaction records, and
article metadata. You want to estimate which recently active customers will
stop purchasing for a week, to help a team prioritize contact. Customer
attributes and individual purchases provide possible context: what someone
bought, through which channel, and how long before the decision it occurred.

This page proposes a retail application with illustrative records. It extends
the [account-outcome pattern](../learn/nested-context-and-account-outcomes.qmd)
to customers; it does not report a measured retention result.

## Define one customer decision

At each daily cutoff, select customers with at least one purchase in
the preceding seven days. Prepare one observation per eligible customer and
cutoff. The target `inactive_next_7_days` is true when that customer makes no
purchase after the cutoff through seven days later.

This is the short-term inactivity formulation in
[RelBench's H&M customer-churn task](https://github.com/snap-stanford/relbench/blob/v1.1.0/relbench/tasks/hm.py#L63-L111).
Its recent-activity requirement is part of the task: a customer who last
purchased a year ago is outside this scoring population. Seven days without a
purchase also need not mean that a customer has permanently left.

Join each transaction to the article attributes available at the cutoff. Keep
the transaction's amount, article, channel, and booking time together in one
record. Customer attributes belong at the root, with their values as known at
that decision. Preserve the customer identifier and cutoff alongside each
observation so results can be associated with the correct decision.

## One observation and its model

For a cutoff of May 28, 2026 at noon UTC, this illustrative training observation
contains two purchases known then. Its label is attached after June 4 at noon,
once the complete seven-day outcome window is available:

```yaml
customer_id: customer-42
cutoff: "2026-05-28T12:00:00Z"
customer_age: 34
club_member_status: ACTIVE
recent_purchases:
  - booked_at: "2026-05-22T12:00:00Z"
    age_days: 6
    article_id: article-17
    article_group: knitwear
    amount: 32.00
    sales_channel: online
  - booked_at: "2026-05-26T12:00:00Z"
    age_days: 2
    article_id: article-03
    article_group: trousers
    amount: 56.20
    sales_channel: store
inactive_next_7_days: true
```

`customer_id` and `cutoff` identify the snapshot for retention and downstream
joins. They stay outside the model fields declared below.

Declare numeric and categorical inputs, a collection of purchase records,
and a Boolean customer target at the root. RelFlow builds the corresponding
encoders and prediction output from this task schema:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.sm(
    customer_age=rf.Number,
    club_member_status=rf.Category,
    recent_purchases=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        age_days=rf.Number,
        article_id=rf.Category,
        article_group=rf.Category,
        amount=rf.Number,
        sales_channel=rf.Category,
    ),
    inactive_next_7_days=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
```

Your application orders purchases oldest to newest; the branch retains the
latest 32 whole records. The model can use article, amount, and channel jointly
within each purchase, alongside the customer's other purchases. `booked_at`
provides calendar cycles. The application-supplied `age_days` expresses elapsed
time from each booking to the cutoff; calendar cycles alone do not express it.

`mask=True` excludes the future inactivity label from the inputs and uses it
as supervision. New requests contain the same customer context and purchases
with `inactive_next_7_days` omitted. Prepare application-owned Parquet files
and follow [Train and save](../learn/train-and-save.qmd),
[Data modules](../guides/data-modules.qmd), and
[Read predictions](../learn/read-predictions.qmd) for the training and
prediction workflow.

After fitting this schema on your application's training and validation
files, save the trained model:

```python
model.save("artifacts/customer-outcomes.rf")
```

[Representation learning](representation-learning.qmd) uses that
application-produced artifact to explore reuse of the customer context.

## Compare the contact decisions

Start with the training population's inactivity rate. Then build a flat
baseline from purchase recency, frequency, spending, and channel summaries,
using a simple classifier or a boosted tree. Compare it with the nested model
on the same customers, cutoffs, histories, and settled labels. A comparison
with extra history available to only one model answers a different question.

Use later decision windows for validation and a separate later test period.
At each historical model-fit time, use only training labels whose complete
outcome windows and reporting delays would have finished by then. Keep those
windows from straddling split boundaries. If the same customer appears at
many cutoffs, report whether the test measures later behavior of existing
customers or performance on unseen customers.

AUROC measures ranking across thresholds; average precision helps assess
ranking when inactivity is uncommon. Also evaluate calibration and precision
or recall at the team's actual contact budget. These checks connect a score
to the proposed outreach policy. Predicting inactivity does not establish
which customers benefit from contact; measure that effect with an
intervention evaluation. [Evaluation](../learn/evaluation.qmd) covers temporal
splits and baseline comparisons.

## Change the outcome deliberately

For **review engagement**, select customers who posted a review in the previous
91 days, then label whether they post no review in the following 91 days.
Use customer attributes and an earlier-review branch containing product,
rating, and review date. This follows the review-activity definition in
[RelBench's Amazon customer-churn task](https://github.com/snap-stanford/relbench/blob/v1.1.0/relbench/tasks/amazon.py#L18-L67).
It measures participation in the review channel: purchasing can continue
without a review. Review recency and frequency provide useful baselines for a
policy that prioritizes invitations for feedback.

For **future spending**, a retailer with complete transaction records could
instead define `spend_next_30_days` as the sum of purchase amounts during the
next 30 days and use a masked `rf.Number` target. Fix currency, refund handling,
and whether the outcome is gross purchases or net revenue before preparing
labels. Compare a training-label median and a recent-spending baseline, then
report MAE in the chosen currency. A 30-day spend estimate has a finite horizon;
calling it lifetime value would require a different definition.

Both variants change the business question, label construction, and evaluation.
Reusing the customer-and-events input pattern does not establish their
predictability. To adapt a trained model, change its target schema, retain
compatible learned state under the
[schema-mutation rules](../guides/schema-mutation.qmd), and fit and evaluate
the new task. Adding an outcome still requires its own settled labels.

## Check what the history leaves out

The scoring population excludes customers without a purchase in the eligibility
window. Missing channels and delayed transactions can turn an apparent absence
into a false inactivity label. Historical membership status and article
attributes must use their values known at the cutoff. Empty history, incomplete
coverage, and a genuine lack of activity require distinct preparation rules.

The 32-purchase cap is an illustrative resource choice; check how often it
truncates customer histories and whether older purchases matter. Nested input
volume still affects memory and serving cost. See
[Prepare observations](../learn/prepare-observations.qmd),
[Preprocessing](../guides/preprocessing.qmd), and
[Performance](../guides/performance.qmd) before choosing production limits.

To turn related tables into deeper observations, continue with
[Relational prediction](relational-prediction.qmd). To rank specific articles
for a customer, see [Recommendations](recommendations.qmd).
